Three readings.

**The offense was worse in the playoffs, by more than the opposition explains.** Across the Jackson-era regular
seasons the Ravens averaged \+0\.089 EPA per play, an elite offense. In their nine playoff
games they averaged \-0\.008, roughly an average one. Some drop is normal: playoff
defenses are better, and they have time to prepare. But the typical playoff offense of these years played about
0\.06 EPA per play worse in January than in its own regular season, and Baltimore fell by
0\.10, close to twice as much. Nor was it simply the quality of the
opponents: in the regular season, against teams that went on to make the playoffs, the Ravens still averaged
\+0\.083, barely below their overall \+0\.089.[^podrop] That part of the narrative is true.

**The run game failed early in the era, and not at the end.** Overall, the Ravens' designed runs fell from
\+0\.08 EPA per play in the regular season to \-0\.02 in the
playoffs, but the diamonds in @fig-playoffs show where that came from. The runs lost value in each of the first four
losses: the Chargers in January 2019 (the seven-defensive-back game), the Titans in January 2020, Buffalo in January
2021 and the Huntley game in Cincinnati in January 2023. They gained value in the last two losses and in all three
wins. Take out just the January 2019 and January 2020 games and the playoff designed runs averaged
\+0\.06. So the early answer to "was the run game solved?" is partly yes, in single games, by
defenses with a week to prepare; the later answer is no.

**The losses came from falling behind and giving the ball away.** The right panel is the mechanism. In the regular
season the Ravens trailed by more than a touchdown on only 10% of their snaps; in the
playoffs, on 37%. They turned the ball over
1\.1 times a game in the regular season and
1\.8 in the playoffs, with three or more turnovers in
4 of the 6 losses. Did the staff abandon the run on its own, or did
the score take it away? The split by score answers it. With the game within a touchdown either way, the Ravens called
designed runs on 47% of their playoff snaps, against 45% in the regular
season: in close games they ran as much as ever. The overall run share fell, from 46%
to 41%, only because they spent so much more of their playoff time behind. That
five-point fall looks small, but it is an average over nine games; in the two worst deficits (January 2020 and
January 2024) the designed-run share was 23% and
18%. This is answer 2 from the last section, playing out
across a decade: a run game built to win close games was asked, again and again, to win from behind.

Look at the losses one at a time and both stories appear. In January 2019 against the Chargers and January 2020
against the Titans, the run game *was* stuffed, and early deficits and turnovers finished the job. In January 2021 at
Buffalo, a 3–3 game at halftime turned late in the third quarter: down 10–3, Jackson drove the Ravens to the Bills'
9 and threw an interception that Taron Johnson returned 101 yards for a touchdown, and two plays later Jackson
left with a concussion, and the Ravens lost 17–3 with Tyler Huntley at quarterback.[^buf21] In January 2024 against
Kansas City, the Ravens trailed 17–7 at halftime and ran only 16 times all game, with their running backs carrying six
of them; their designed runs averaged \+0\.17 EPA, better than their
regular-season average, and they lost 17–10 after three turnovers.[^afcg] In January 2025 at Buffalo they ran for 176
yards and still lost 27–25, after an interception, a fumble on a sack and a Mark Andrews fumble, then a failed
two-point conversion that would have tied the game.[^buf25] The later losses look less like a scheme being solved
and more like an offense built on the run being taken out of it by the scoreboard.

How much of that is bad luck? Some, certainly: nine games, about 597 plays, is a
small sample, and turnovers in particular are noisy from game to game. But a pattern repeated across six seasons,
four lead running backs (Gus Edwards, Ingram, Dobbins and Henry) and three coordinators (Mornhinweg, Roman and
Monken) deserves an explanation, and the most honest one is this: the pistol option offense was at its best
protecting a lead or playing even, and the games it lost were the games where it had to do the thing it was built to
do least. The 2023 change of coordinator was, in part, an attempt to fix exactly that.

::: {.callout-note title="Madden vs. real life"}
In a video game, a great offense is great in every situation, because you can call any play from any score. Real
offenses are built for a *range* of situations: personnel, practice time and a quarterback's skills all get spent
on the situations the staff expects most. An offense built to run is spending its practice week on runs, and when
it falls behind by fourteen, it is asking players to win with the part of the playbook they practised least. That
is a trade-off, not a flaw, and every offense makes one.
:::

## The Monken changes (2023)

After the 2022 season Greg Roman left. The Ravens' offense under him had ranked first, seventh, 17th and 19th in
points in his four years as coordinator, and the passing game had never quite caught up to the run.[^romanexit]
In February 2023 Baltimore hired **Todd Monken**, who had just won two straight national championships as
Georgia's offensive coordinator and had run NFL offenses in Tampa Bay and Cleveland.[^monken]

Monken's mandate was to make Jackson a quarterback who could win from the pocket, without throwing away what made
him dangerous. @fig-fingerprint shows what he did:

- **From the pistol to the shotgun.** Pistol snaps fell from 26% of plays
  in 2022 to 7% in 2023, and the shotgun rose to
  78%.[^loc] The shotgun gives the quarterback a better view of the
  coverage and a faster launch, at the cost of the pistol's downhill back and its lack of a tell.
- **Fewer designed quarterback runs.** Jackson's designed runs fell from 5\.5 a game to
  4\.1. He still ran, but more of it was scrambling, improvising when a pass play broke
  down, rather than running on purpose.
- **More receivers, and more passing on early downs.** The Ravens drafted receiver Zay Flowers in the first round,
  used three-receiver sets more, and on neutral early downs ran the ball on 43% of
  plays, 27th in the league, after ranking first in that category in 2019.

The result was a career-high 3,678 passing yards for Jackson and his second MVP award, won with 49 of 50 first-place
votes, and a 13–4 record and the AFC's top seed.[^mvp23] The run game didn't collapse without the
volume of quarterback runs. It ranked 3rd in EPA per designed run, and the
Ravens still led the league in rushing yards. The likeliest reason is that the threat was doing some of the work the
carries used to do: a backside end who had to respect Jackson every snap was still frozen, whether Jackson ran six
times or four. Play-by-play can't see a frozen end, but it can see the runs Jackson didn't carry, and they held up.
Baltimore's designed runs by its running backs and receivers averaged \+0\.002 EPA in 2023,
5th in the league and well above the league's \-0\.08; in
Roman's last season, with more Jackson carries, they had ranked 9th.[^nq]

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: AFC Championship, Kansas City at Baltimore, January 28, 2024"}
The Ravens beat Houston 34–10 in the divisional round, then hosted the Chiefs for a trip to the Super Bowl. They lost
17–10, and the game became the sharpest criticism of the Monken offense: Baltimore ran only 16 times, and its
running backs carried just six of those.[^afcg2]

**What to notice:** the first half and the turnovers, not the play-calling alone. Kansas City led 17–7 at halftime,
and the Ravens turned the ball over three times: a fumble on a sack in the second quarter, then, in the fourth, Zay
Flowers's fumble at the Kansas City 1-yard line and an interception in the end zone. Watch Steve Spagnuolo's defense on Jackson's dropbacks: four-man rushes,
disguised coverages, and rushers who kept their lanes so that Jackson's scrambles went nowhere. Then ask the question
the chapter keeps asking: was the run abandoned, or was it taken away by the scoreboard? The answer is some of both,
and it was the last time the Ravens' run game rested mainly on Jackson.
:::

## The Derrick Henry seasons (2024–2025)

In March 2024 the Ravens signed **Derrick Henry**, the 30-year-old former Titans back who had run for 2,027 yards
in 2020 and had beaten them almost single-handedly in that January 2020 playoff game, on a two-year
contract.[^henry] It was a signing that made the threat run both ways. For five years, defenses had to decide whom to
fear on a read: the quarterback or a good running back. Now the back was one of the most punishing runners of his
generation, a 247-pound back who had led the league in rushing twice.

**2024 was the best offense of the era.** Henry ran for 1,921 yards and 16 touchdowns, second in the league in
yards behind Saquon Barkley's 2,005; Jackson threw for 4,172 yards, 41 touchdowns and only four interceptions; and
Baltimore led the NFL in EPA per play, in rushing yards, and, again, in EPA per designed run.[^h24] The team went
12–5, beat Pittsburgh in the wild-card round as Henry ran for 186 yards, and lost at Buffalo,
the game described above.

**The run game moved under center.** The data shows how differently the Henry offense was built. The Ravens took
28% of their 2024 snaps with Jackson under center, nearly three times their
2022 rate, and 45% of their designed runs started there.

Why under center, after five years of selling the pistol, and for the most downhill back in the league? The pistol
and the I-formation both put the back about seven yards deep, so depth isn't the difference. The differences are
what happens at the mesh and what the defense can see.

- *A straight track to the hole.* From the pistol the quarterback stands four yards deep, directly in the back's way,
  so the back has to bend around his hip to take the handoff. From under center the quarterback opens out of the
  back's path and hands off on the move, and the back runs his zone or duo track with his shoulders square to the
  line. That was the game Henry had built his career on: from 2019 to 2023 no player ran for more yards with his
  quarterback under center (5,795, by ESPN's count). His former Tennessee teammate Taylor Lewan said publicly that
  Henry wanted to run downhill and disliked turning his shoulder on read plays, although Henry himself said he was
  comfortable with them.[^henryuc]
- *Play-action with the quarterback's back to the defense.* Under center, the quarterback turns away from the line
  to fake the handoff, so linebackers and safeties can't see the ball, and the fake to a back as feared as Henry
  holds them longer. Henry's Titans had averaged more yards per play-action pass than any other team since 2016, and
  the Ravens' \+0\.31 EPA per dropback in 2024 ranked 1st
  in the league.
- *A quarterback who was now a passer first.* Monken had already moved Jackson's game toward the pocket. With Henry
  carrying the load, the offense no longer needed Jackson's legs on every snap, and under center it no longer had
  to show them.

What it gave up was the read: from under center the quarterback can't easily read an end and keep the ball. So the
read game didn't vanish; it became a change-up, and it kept its sting. Henry's carries from the pistol,
92 of them across the two seasons, averaged
7\.8 yards and \+0\.21 EPA, against
5\.1 yards and \+0\.09 EPA from under
center.[^henryloc] Read that comparison with care. It is a small sample, and a change-up is called when the staff
thinks the defense is set up for it, so its numbers flatter it; the same play called on every snap would not average
that much. But it is the read offense in miniature: an end who has to stay home for Jackson is an end who isn't
chasing Henry.

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Pittsburgh at Baltimore, January 11, 2025 (wild-card round)"}
The Henry offense at its best. Baltimore beat Pittsburgh 28–14, called designed runs on
64% of its plays, and never trailed; Henry carried 26 times
for 186 yards.[^pit24]

**What to notice:** Jackson's alignment before each run. Under center, watch the back's track and the
second level: the linebackers have to fit Henry's downhill run, not a read. Then watch for the snaps in the pistol or
shotgun, the change-up, and for the backside end on them: he can't chase Henry, because the quarterback might keep.
Two offenses, one game, and the defense has to be ready for both.
:::

**2025 was the end.** Jackson missed four games, three with a hamstring injury in October and one with a back
injury in December, and was less of a runner when he played, saying afterwards that his health had limited his
mobility:[^lj25] by this chapter's count 28 designed runs in
13 games, about two a game.
Henry still ran for more than 1,500 yards, the run game still ranked 3rd in
EPA per designed run, and the Ravens ran on early downs more than all but one team. But a 1–5 start, a defense that
gave up 398 points, and a 26–24 loss at Pittsburgh in Week 18 with the division on the line left them
8–9 and out of the playoffs.[^s25] On January 6, 2026, the Ravens fired John Harbaugh after 18
seasons.

## What survives: the era closed, and the 2026 epilogue

The coaches have scattered. Harbaugh is the Giants' head coach in 2026, Monken is the Browns' head coach, and Roman
spent 2024 and 2025 as Jim Harbaugh's offensive coordinator with the Chargers, who fired him in
January 2026.[^roman26] The 2026 Ravens belong to **Jesse Minter**, a Ravens assistant from 2017 to 2020 and the Chargers'
defensive coordinator in 2024 and 2025, as head
coach, with **Declan Doyle**, who came from Ben Johnson's Chicago staff, as offensive coordinator and **Anthony
Weaver** as defensive coordinator.[^staff2026] Jackson is still the quarterback. What Doyle builds around him is a
2026 story, and this book's coverage stops at the end of the 2025 season, so whether his Ravens line up in the pistol,
the shotgun or under center is a question for your own Sunday viewing. The Watch-for-it list below is how to answer it.

What survives the era is bigger than one team.

- **The arithmetic is now conventional wisdom.** "Count the quarterback as a blocker" was an option coach's slogan
  in 2018. By 2025 it was how every NFL defense planned for Jalen Hurts, Josh Allen and Jayden Daniels, and how every
  analyst explained why those offenses ran well against light boxes.
- **Heavy personnel came back.** In 2025 NFL offenses used fewer than three receivers on 41.7% of plays, the most
  since Next Gen Stats began tracking.[^heavy25] The Ravens weren't the only cause (the 49ers, Rams and Eagles all
  pushed the same way), but they showed that a modern offense could live in 12, 21 and 22 personnel and still throw.
- **The quarterback run became a managed resource.** The Ravens' own data tells the story of the last seven years in
  miniature: from seven or eight designed runs a game in 2019 to about two in 2025, with the efficiency of the run
  game barely moving. The lesson the league took is that a running quarterback's value is mostly in the *threat*,
  which can be spent a few carries at a time, on the downs and in the games where it matters, and saved the rest of
  the time.
- **The pistol didn't.** The pistol as a *base* alignment was a Ravens thing, and it left with Roman. It survives as a
  run-heavy niche look (02-02's data has a few teams living in it), and as a change-up that offenses built around
  the shotgun or under center use when they want a read, as the Henry-era Ravens did. That is a good example of the course's larger point: the principle (an extra blocker,
  either side, no tell) outlived its favourite formation.

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it"}
**On Sunday: count the defenders against a running quarterback.** Any team with a quarterback who runs, Baltimore
or not, will do.

*Before the snap*

- **Count the blockers:** five linemen, plus every tight end and fullback near the line.
- **Count the box:** the [box count](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-box-count) is every defender within about 5–7 yards of the line and inside the tight ends.
- **Add the quarterback.** If he's in the pistol or shotgun with a back beside or behind him and is a real runner,
  add one to the offense's side. Now compare: more defenders than blockers-plus-one, and the defense has its
  plus-one; even, and the defense's extra man has to come from a safety.
- **Find where the extra man is.** A safety walked down at eight yards, or a single deep safety in the middle? Then
  the play-action pass is aimed at him.
- **Where is the back?** Directly behind the quarterback (pistol): no directional tell. Beside him: note the side.
  On zone runs and zone reads the run *usually* goes the other way; gap runs from the shotgun often go to the back's
  side, so look for a puller before you commit.

*At the snap*

- **Watch the two ends.** The one nobody touches is being read. Does he stay home (give coming) or chase (keep
  coming)?
- **Look for a puller.** A guard pulling toward the unblocked end: power read. A guard and a tight end pulling the
  same way while the quarterback *and* the back step the other way: QB counter. The same two pullers with the *back*
  following them: counter read or counter bash, with the quarterback reading an end.

*After the play*

- On the replay, check the backside end on a plain handoff. Did he chase the cutback, or stay home for a quarterback
  who didn't have the ball? Count how often he stays, over a quarter. That is the hidden yardage.
- Note the score. Is the offense still running when it's behind by two scores? That's the question that decided the
  Ravens' playoff games.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 1: eight in the box.** First-and-10 at midfield, first quarter, tied. Baltimore is in the pistol with two
tight ends; the defense walks a safety down and shows eight in the box with one deep safety. Count the blockers
and the box with Jackson as a runner. Who is the defense's extra man, and which Ravens play does this picture
invite?

::: {#cell-fig-drill-1 .cell execution_count=11}
``` {.python .cell-code}
dfn = [D("SS", "SS", 1.6, 6.8, "SS") if q.key == "PE" else q for q in front62(fs=True)]
p = Play(pistol(), dfn, los=60, to_go=10, title="Drill 1: 1st and 10, midfield")
f = draw(p, lateral=(-10.0, 10.5), window=(-8.6, 14.6), width_in=4.8)
box_shade(f, p, 0.2, 5.6, -7.6, 8.3)
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Drill 1: pistol 12 personnel against an eight-man box and a single deep safety. The strong safety (SS) has walked down outside the right tight end to play the edge, the job a 9-technique would do (the wide receivers and cornerbacks are out of the picture).](12-05-ravens-lamar-run-game_files/figure-html/fig-drill-1-output-1.svg){#fig-drill-1}
:::
:::


:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Seven blockers plus Jackson's read against eight: a hat on every hat.** Five linemen and two tight ends make seven
blockers. The box has eight: five linemen, the walked-down strong safety on the right edge, and two linebackers. On a handoff with a pocket quarterback the defense
would be plus-one. With Jackson reading one end, it is even (@fig-fit-two-qbs, @fig-pistol-iv).

**The defense's extra man is the free safety**, the only defender not in the box and the only one deep. If he comes
down to stop the run, there is nobody behind the linebackers.

**What it invites: both, and that's the point.** A read is fine: the box is even, and the 2019 Ravens ran well
against eight-man boxes all season. But eight in the box against the Ravens meant the defense had spent its last
spare man, so this is also the look a **play-action pass at the deep middle** is built for: a fake to the back that
holds the linebackers and the safety for a beat, with a tight end up the seam behind them (@fig-13-plate, left). A
defense that shows this picture can't be right about both, which is why the Ravens could call either.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 2: read the 9.** Same look, a moment after the snap. The line is blocking power to the right: the tight end
and tackle have blocked down, the left guard is pulling. The play-side 9 has not been touched. He has stepped
hard *inside*, toward the hole. The back is coming around Jackson's right hip and sweeping wide. Give or keep? And if the read is
right, who has to make the tackle?

::: {#cell-fig-drill-2 .cell execution_count=12}
``` {.python .cell-code}
dfn = [q.moved(d=1.6, w=5.6) if q.key == "PE" else q for q in front62(fs=True)]
p = Play(pistol(), dfn, los=60, to_go=10, title="Drill 2: the 9 squeezes")
go_to(p, "Y", (0.4, 4.1), via=[(-0.3, 4.5)])
go_to(p, "RT", (0.5, 2.7), via=[(-0.4, 3.0)])
go_to(p, "RG", (3.7, -1.6), via=[(-0.2, 1.9), (0.4, 2.0), (1.4, 0.8)])
go_to(p, "C", (0.4, -0.5))
go_to(p, "LT", (0.3, -3.8), via=[(-0.6, -3.5)])
go_to(p, "U", (0.4, -6.0), via=[(-0.4, -5.3)])
go_to(p, "LG", (3.4, 2.9), "pull", via=[(-2.2, -1.3), (-2.7, 0.9), (-1.9, 3.4), (-0.3, 4.7), (1.6, 4.3)])
go_to(p, "RB", (-4.0, 3.6), "path", via=[(-5.0, 0.6), (-4.4, 1.4)])
p.highlight("PE", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, lateral=(-10.0, 13.0), window=(-8.6, 14.2), width_in=5.0)
x0, y0 = _P(f, p, 1.0, 8.6)
x1, y1 = _P(f, p, 1.4, 6.8)
f.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((float(x0), float(y0)), (float(x1), float(y1)), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=10,
                               color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.6, zorder=6))
point_to(f, p, (4.2, 9.6), (1.5, 7.2), "the 9 squeezes\ninside", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
read_line(f, p, (-4.0, 0.3), (0.6, 5.0))
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Drill 2: the pistol power read a moment after the snap. The play-side 9 (ringed) has squeezed inside from where he lined up (his short arrow). Every block is drawn as its full assignment: the down blocks, the right guard's climb to the Will and the left guard's pull for the Mike. The back (thin arrow) is coming around the quarterback's right hip.](12-05-ravens-lamar-run-game_files/figure-html/fig-drill-2-output-1.svg){#fig-drill-2}
:::
:::


:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Give.** The 9 has squeezed inside, toward the hole the quarterback would run through: he has taken the keep away
himself. So Jackson hands the ball to the back, who is already running outside the 9 at full speed (@fig-pistol-iv).

**Who has to tackle him?** Probably nobody in the box. Every other box defender has a blocker assigned (the down
blocks, the right guard climbing to the Will, the pulling guard leading for the Mike), and the 9 is inside the
runner. The one box defender with a chance is the Mike, if he reads the play fast and beats the pulling guard over
the top, which is why a give is never a sure thing. Otherwise the tackle has to come from **outside or behind**: the cornerback on that side (if the wide receiver hasn't blocked
him) or the free safety, coming from 12 yards deep across the field. That is the power read's promise, a running
back in space against a defensive back, and its risk: if the corner or safety arrives in time and the back was
running sideways, the gain is small.

If the 9 had **widened** with the back instead, the answer flips: keep, and Jackson runs inside him behind the
pulling guard.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 3: down fourteen.** Second-and-8 at your own 30, early in the third quarter of a playoff game. You're down 14.
The defense shows two deep safeties and only six in the box. Your quarterback is a great runner; your offense has
the league's best run game. Does the box say run? Does the scoreboard? What would you call, and what does the
Ravens' history say about the trap in this picture?

::: {#cell-fig-drill-3 .cell execution_count=13}
``` {.python .cell-code}
off = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, 2.1, "R"), O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"),
                 O("X", "WR", -0.7, -15.0, "X"), O("H", "WR", -1.5, -9.0, "H"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 14.5, "Z")]
check_legal(off)
dfn = [D("LE", "DE", 1.0, -4.1, "5"), D("DT1", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "1"), D("DT3", "DT", 1.0, 2.4, "3"),
       D("RE", "DE", 1.0, 5.6, "9"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 5.0, 1.6, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 5.0, -2.4, "W"),
       D("NB", "NB", 5.0, -8.6, "NB"), D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -15.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 14.5, "CB"),
       D("FS", "FS", 13.0, -7.0, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 13.0, 7.0, "SS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=8, title="Drill 3: 2nd and 8, down 14, third quarter")
f = draw(p, lateral=(-18.0, 17.5), window=(-8.0, 15.6), width_in=5.6)
box_shade(f, p, 0.2, 6.0, -6.4, 7.0)
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Drill 3: shotgun 11 personnel (one tight end, three receivers) against a two-high shell with six in the box; the offense is down 14 early in the third quarter.](12-05-ravens-lamar-run-game_files/figure-html/fig-drill-3-output-1.svg){#fig-drill-3}
:::
:::


:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**The box says run.** It is a [light box](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-light-box): six defenders against six blockers (five linemen and the tight end) and a quarterback who reads:
the offense is effectively plus-one. Against light boxes, efficient running teams do well, and the Ravens were the most
efficient running team of their era (@fig-rush-epa).

**The scoreboard says "don't panic."** Down 14 with more than a quarter and a half to play is two possessions, not a
two-minute drill. A good run on second-and-8 is a good play in any quarter, and this two-high shell is inviting you to
throw: if you throw against two deep safeties and five underneath (the nickel, both linebackers and both corners,
with four rushing), you are throwing into the coverage the defense chose. (The win-probability tools of
[13-03](../13-analytics-and-data/13-03-win-probability-and-fourth-down.qmd) make this precise.)

**But is running really better for this team?** That is the comparison that decides it, and it isn't automatic:
[10-01](../10-situational-football/10-01-early-downs-and-field-zones.qmd) showed that passing is usually the more
efficient choice, and the 2019 Ravens' dropbacks (\+0\.32 EPA) were worth more per play than
their runs (\+0\.11). Two things tip this snap toward the run. The box: against six or
fewer, Baltimore's designed runs averaged \+0\.09 EPA across 2019–2025, against the league's
\-0\.02. And the score: in the Jackson-era regular seasons, when the Ravens trailed by more than a
touchdown, their designed runs averaged \+0\.11 EPA and their dropbacks \+0\.06, because a
defense protecting a lead plays pass and leaves the box light.[^trail]

**The trap** is the one in @fig-playoffs: a deficit that pulls a run team off the run, and the turnovers that come
with throwing from behind. The right call here is the run the defense is conceding (a read, or a designed run with
the back blocking), and the right *plan* is to stay patient for another series. The two-score deficit becomes a
three-score deficit far more often from an interception than from a three-yard run.
:::

## Takeaways

- The 2019–2022 Ravens built a **pistol option offense**: the pistol as the base alignment, heavy personnel, a menu of
  option reads and designed quarterback runs, so that the defense had to account for one more ball carrier on every
  snap.
- A running quarterback changes **every** run fit, not just the reads: the end he might read has to stay home on plain
  handoffs too, every defender's fit gets a "quarterback" line, and backside pursuit stops being free. An eight-man
  box against him is a seven-man box.
- The signature plays each make a defender's textbook reaction wrong: the **pistol inverted veer** (squeeze the hole
  and the back runs outside you), **13 personnel** (play it as a run formation and the seam opens; Baltimore threw
  from it two times in three), and the **QB counter** (follow the first flow and the play goes back the other way).
- The data fingerprint: Baltimore's designed runs were above the league average **every season** from 2018 to 2025,
  top three in six of them, under two coordinators and five lead backs. What changed was the recipe: pistol and
  quarterback runs under Roman, the shotgun and fewer designed runs under **Monken (2023)**, under-center runs with
  **Derrick Henry (2024–2025)**, chosen for his downhill track and for play-action, with the pistol read kept as a
  change-up.
- Defenses answered with speed, pressure, spies, the everyday option answers and, most effectively, **the
  scoreboard**. In the playoffs (3–5 with Jackson) the offense fell off by about twice the usual playoff drop. Early in
  the era prepared defenses stuffed the run in single games; later, the losses came from deficits and turnovers.
  In close playoff games the Ravens ran as often as ever.
- The era closed in January 2026 with Harbaugh's firing. What survives is the arithmetic (count the quarterback as a
  blocker), heavy personnel, and the idea that a running quarterback's value is mostly the threat, spent a few carries
  at a time.

**From the simulation to real tracking data.** The QB counter animation in this chapter is a gridiron simulation
written in NFL Big Data Bowl coordinates (simulated, BDB-format), so real tracking frames drop into the same drawing
code. The Big Data Bowl releases carry the play-by-play description of each play, so finding a Jackson designed run
is a text search (`"L.Jackson"` as the rusher, no "scramble"), and the pre-snap frames of the 2025 edition show
whether he was in the pistol. The cell below, folded on the website and not run (the course does not download the
Big Data Bowl files), shows the shape of that code.

::: {#a08afb71 .cell execution_count=14}
``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Show the Python (real tracking data; not run)"}
import pandas as pd
from gridiron import bdb, show_animation

trk = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb/tracking_week_*.csv")       # BDB 2025: 2022 season, weeks 1-9
plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/plays.csv")
runs = plays[(plays["possessionTeam"] == "BAL") & plays["playDescription"].str.contains("L.Jackson")
             & ~plays["playDescription"].str.contains("scramble|pass", case=False)]
one = bdb.prepare(trk, plays, game_id=runs["gameId"].iloc[0], play_id=runs["playId"].iloc[0])
show_animation(one, times=[0.0, 0.6, 1.9, 2.7])                 # the same four moments as the simulation
```
